Hosea 1: Hosea prophesies to northern Israel in the days of Jeroboam II of Israel and of Uzziah through Hezekiah of Judah (Hosea 1:1), about 755–715 BC. His son is named Jezreel, after the valley where Jehu killed Ahab's house (2 Kings 9–10).
Hosea 2: Israel is pictured as an unfaithful wife who credits Baal for her grain, wine, and oil.
Hosea 3: Hosea buys back his wife for fifteen pieces of silver and barley (Hosea 3:2).
Hosea 4: Hosea condemns priests and worship at Gilgal and Bethaven, his name for Bethel (Hosea 4:15).
Hosea 5: Ephraim goes to Assyria and to king Jareb for help (Hosea 5:13). Israel's last kings paid tribute to Assyria (2 Kings 15:19–20).
Hosea 6: Hosea names crimes in Gilead and on the road to Shechem (Hosea 6:8–9).
Hosea 7: "All their kings are fallen" (Hosea 7:7): four of Israel's last six kings were assassinated (2 Kings 15). Ephraim calls to Egypt and goes to Assyria (Hosea 7:11).
Hosea 8: Hosea condemns the calf of Samaria and the kings Israel set up without God (Hosea 8:4–6).
Hosea 9: Hosea warns that Ephraim will return to Egypt and eat unclean food in Assyria (Hosea 9:3), and recalls "the days of Gibeah" (Hosea 9:9).
Hosea 10: The calf of Bethaven will be carried to Assyria as a present for king Jareb (Hosea 10:5–6). Shalman's destruction of Betharbel is mentioned (Hosea 10:14).
Hosea 11: "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt" (Hosea 11:1).
Hosea 12: Hosea recalls Jacob at the Jabbok and at Bethel, and Ephraim's treaty with Assyria and oil sent to Egypt (Hosea 12:1).
Hosea 13: Hosea warns, "Samaria shall become desolate" (Hosea 13:16). Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC.
Hosea 14: The book ends with a call to return and say, "Asshur shall not save us" (Hosea 14:3).
Joel 1: "The word of the LORD that came to Joel the son of Pethuel" (Joel 1:1). Joel gives no date. A locust plague strips Judah's vines and fig trees, and offerings at the temple are cut off.
Joel 2: The locusts are described as an army. The priests are called to gather the people at Zion for a fast.
Joel 3: The nations are gathered to "the valley of Jehoshaphat" (Joel 3:2). Tyre, Sidon, and the Philistines have sold Judeans to the Grecians (Joel 3:6).
Amos 1: Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah, prophesies to northern Israel "two years before the earthquake" in the days of Uzziah and Jeroboam II (Amos 1:1), about 760 BC. Zechariah 14:5 recalls the same earthquake.
Amos 2: The oracles against Israel's neighbors end with Judah and then Israel itself.
Amos 3: Amos calls Ashdod and Egypt to witness the disorder in Samaria (Amos 3:9) and speaks of its winter and summer houses and houses of ivory (Amos 3:15). Carved ivories have been excavated at Samaria.
Amos 4: Amos addresses the "kine of Bashan" in the mountain of Samaria (Amos 4:1) and mocks worship at Bethel and Gilgal.
Amos 5: Amos tells Israel not to seek Bethel, Gilgal, or Beersheba (Amos 5:5).
Amos 6: "Woe to them that are at ease in Zion" (Amos 6:1); the wealthy lie on beds of ivory. Amos names Calneh, Hamath, and Gath.
Amos 7: Amaziah, priest of Bethel, "the king's chapel" (Amos 7:13), reports Amos to Jeroboam II and tells him to go back to Judah.
Amos 8: Amos sees a basket of summer fruit. He condemns merchants who make the ephah small and the shekel great.
Amos 9: Amos sees the LORD beside the altar. The book ends with the promise to raise up "the tabernacle of David that is fallen" (Amos 9:11).
Obadiah 1: The vision concerns Edom, which rejoiced and joined in when Jerusalem was plundered (Obadiah 1:11–14). Edom's capital Sela was in the rocky hills south of the Dead Sea. The book gives no date.
Jonah 1: Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet in the time of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25), boards a ship at Joppa bound for Tarshish, in the far west, instead of going to Nineveh.
Jonah 2: Jonah prays from inside the fish for three days and three nights.
Jonah 3: Jonah goes to Nineveh, "an exceeding great city of three days' journey" (Jonah 3:3), on the Tigris in Assyria.
Jonah 4: Jonah sits east of Nineveh in a booth to see what will happen to the city.
Micah 1: Micah of Moresheth, a town in Judah's lowland, prophesies in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (Micah 1:1), about 740–700 BC. He names Samaria and towns of the Shephelah, including Lachish.
Micah 2: Micah condemns those who covet and seize fields and houses (Micah 2:2).
Micah 3: Micah warns, "Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field" (Micah 3:12). Elders quote this in Jeremiah 26:18 as spoken in Hezekiah's days.
Micah 4: Micah 4:1–3 is nearly the same as Isaiah 2:2–4. The chapter also names Babylon (Micah 4:10).
Micah 5: Micah names "Bethlehem Ephratah" (Micah 5:2) and the land of Assyria and of Nimrod (Micah 5:6).
Micah 6: God recalls bringing Israel from Egypt and the story of Balak and Balaam (Micah 6:4–5).
Micah 7: The book closes with God's mercy and his oath "unto our fathers from the days of old" (Micah 7:20).
Nahum 1: "The burden of Nineveh" (Nahum 1:1), capital of Assyria. Nahum is from Elkosh, a town of unknown location.
Nahum 2: The poem describes the fall of Nineveh, with chariots in the streets. Babylonians and Medes destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC.
Nahum 3: Nineveh is compared to No (Thebes) in Egypt (Nahum 3:8), which Assyria sacked in 663 BC, so the book dates between 663 and 612 BC.
Habakkuk 1: God says he is raising up "the Chaldeans" (Habakkuk 1:6), the Babylonians, who rose to power after 626 BC and defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC.
Habakkuk 2: Habakkuk stands on his watch and is told to write the vision plainly on tables (Habakkuk 2:1–2).
Habakkuk 3: Habakkuk's prayer is set to Shigionoth and describes God coming from Teman and mount Paran (Habakkuk 3:3).
Zephaniah 1: Zephaniah, a descendant of Hezekiah, prophesies in the days of Josiah (Zephaniah 1:1), about 640–609 BC. He names Baal worship and the Chemarims (idol priests) in Jerusalem (Zephaniah 1:4).
Zephaniah 2: Zephaniah prophesies against Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, and Ekron, against Moab and Ammon, Ethiopia, and Assyria; Nineveh will become a desolation (Zephaniah 2:13).
Zephaniah 3: "Woe to her that is filthy and polluted, to the oppressing city!" (Zephaniah 3:1). The book ends with God gathering his people.
Haggai 1: On the first day of the sixth month of Darius's second year (Haggai 1:1), August 520 BC, Haggai tells Zerubbabel and Joshua that the temple still lies in ruins. Work begins twenty-four days later (Haggai 1:15).
Haggai 2: On the twenty-first of the seventh month, during the feast of tabernacles, Haggai compares the new temple with Solomon's. Two more messages come on the twenty-fourth of the ninth month (Haggai 2:1, 10, 20).
Zechariah 1: Zechariah, grandson of Iddo, begins prophesying in the eighth month of Darius's second year (Zechariah 1:1), 520 BC, two months after Haggai. His night visions are dated to the eleventh month (Zechariah 1:7), February 519 BC.
Zechariah 2: A man with a measuring line measures Jerusalem, which will be inhabited "as towns without walls" (Zechariah 2:4).
Zechariah 3: Joshua the high priest, who led worship alongside Zerubbabel (Ezra 3:2), stands before the angel in filthy garments.
Zechariah 4: Zechariah sees a golden candlestick and two olive trees. Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, has laid the temple's foundation and will finish it (Zechariah 4:9).
Zechariah 5: Zechariah sees a flying roll and a woman in an ephah carried to "the land of Shinar" (Zechariah 5:11), Babylonia.
Zechariah 6: Four chariots go out, and silver and gold from returned exiles of Babylon are made into crowns for Joshua (Zechariah 6:10–11).
Zechariah 7: In the fourth year of Darius, ninth month (Zechariah 7:1), 518 BC, men from Bethel ask whether to keep fasting in the fifth month, as they have for seventy years.
Zechariah 8: God promises that the fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months will become feasts (Zechariah 8:19); they marked stages of Jerusalem's siege and fall (Jeremiah 52:4; 39:2; 52:12; 41:1–2).
Zechariah 9: Chapters 9–14 have no dates. Scholars debate whether Zechariah wrote them later in life or others added them. This oracle names Hadrach, Damascus, Tyre, the Philistine cities, and "thy sons, O Greece" (Zechariah 9:13).
Zechariah 10: The oracle promises to bring Ephraim back from Egypt and Assyria to Gilead and Lebanon (Zechariah 10:10).
Zechariah 11: The shepherd is paid thirty pieces of silver and casts them "to the potter in the house of the LORD" (Zechariah 11:13). Matthew 27:9–10 refers to this.
Zechariah 12: The oracle describes mourning in Jerusalem like "the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon" (Zechariah 12:11), where Josiah was killed.
Zechariah 13: A fountain is opened for the house of David; prophets will be ashamed of their visions.
Zechariah 14: The book ends with the mount of Olives split and all nations keeping the feast of tabernacles in Jerusalem. It recalls the earthquake "in the days of Uzziah" (Zechariah 14:5).
Malachi 1: Malachi speaks to Jerusalem after the temple has been rebuilt. Priests offer blemished animals they would not dare give "thy governor" (Malachi 1:8), a Persian official, in the 5th century BC.
Malachi 2: Malachi rebukes priests and men who divorce "the wife of thy youth" (Malachi 2:14). Nehemiah 13 deals with similar problems in Jerusalem around 433 BC.
Malachi 3: Malachi says the people rob God in tithes and offerings (Malachi 3:8), as Nehemiah 13:10–12 also records.
Malachi 4: The book and the Old Testament end with Elijah promised "before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD" (Malachi 4:5). About four hundred years pass before the New Testament.
